description: Fire Fire Busters is a team of full-stack and agentic AI builders taking on Flame in Freefall. We aim to turn NASA’s microgravity combustion research into a trustworthy, interactive fire-safety intelligence platform with traceable evidence—not just another chatbot. We’re looking for teammates with combustion/fire science, aerospace, data analysis, scientific research, UI/UX, or storytelling skills. Join us to help make future Moon and Mars missions safer.
summary:
FlameTrace is an evidence-first research observatory that transforms complex NASA microgravity-combustion resources into interactive, traceable insights. Developed for the “Flame in Free Fall” challenge, it integrates reviewed evidence from PSI-117, PSI-159, and PSI-26, covering droplet combustion, gaseous cool flames, and solid-material fire suppression.

Users can filter and compare experimental runs, inspect cited chart points, explore suppression outcomes, export selected records, and question an AI assistant grounded in retrieved NASA evidence. The assistant improves technical search queries, identifies relevant records and document passages, highlights unknowns, validates citations, and links important claims to their original NASA page or data row.

Our current workspace contains 300 structured experiment records, 721 citations, 1,073 searchable evidence passages, and 205 reviewed chart points. FlameTrace helps researchers and engineers identify relevant investigations and usable variables more efficiently while preserving provenance and scientific limitations—supporting future spacecraft fire detection, material screening, and suppression research.
details:
FlameTrace is an evidence-first research observatory that makes NASA microgravity-combustion data easier to discover, compare, visualize, and verify. Rather than functioning as a general-purpose chatbot, it provides purpose-built research experiences for different forms of combustion evidence.

The current workspace contains three reviewed NASA investigations: PSI-159 for gaseous cool-flame experiments, PSI-26 for burning and suppression of solid materials, and PSI-117 for droplet-combustion history.

NASA reports, spreadsheets, experimental tables, and numerical records are processed through a local ingestion pipeline. It preserves the original files, normalizes selected fields, records missing values, creates stable source and citation identifiers, and prepares searchable passages and structured experimental records.

Users can filter experiments by fuel, material, or outcome; visualize pressure, fuel flow, and reported burn duration; select exact runs for comparison; explore airflow and nitrogen-suppression observations; inspect 205 cited droplet-history measurements; export selected records; and open the original evidence behind a value or conclusion.

FlameTrace also includes an evidence-aware AI assistant. For a research question, the AI determines whether retrieval is necessary and improves the search query without removing user-supplied facts. It then performs a bounded hybrid search across structured records, document passages, semantic similarity, and keywords. Selected experiments can be attached directly to a question. The answer is generated only from the retrieved evidence, and its citation identifiers are validated before display. Casual messages such as greetings bypass retrieval.

FlameTrace helps researchers move from a broad fire-safety question to a relevant NASA investigation, experiment, chart point, and source record. Its intended impact is to support spacecraft fire detection, material screening, suppression research, predictive modeling, and safer crewed habitats. It is a research-support tool, not an operational fire-control system, and it does not invent universal safety thresholds from incomplete evidence.

The frontend uses React, TypeScript, Recharts, and TanStack Query and is deployed through Vercel. The backend uses Python and FastAPI and is deployed through Render. Supabase provides PostgreSQL, pgvector semantic search, and private storage. The AI layer has a provider-switchable, OpenAI-compatible configuration.

Our creative contribution is the combination of three specialized interactive laboratories with an evidence-aware AI assistant. Condition maps, synchronized selections, point-level chart inspection, cited exports, and source-linked answers transform static research archives into an explorable workspace. We prioritized scientific provenance, explicit unknowns, citation accuracy, responsive design, rate limiting, provider flexibility, and honest disclosure of the project’s current dataset coverage.
